intrinsic_value_estimate: $54-64 per share in the base case, using owner earnings. 1988 owner earnings are estimated at about $2.60 per share (range $2.40-2.80): net income plus depreciation less estimated maintenance capex, adjusted for retained affiliate earnings. They are assumed to grow 13% a year for 10 years, with the stock valued at 15x owner earnings in 1998 and the value discounted at 10-12% (bond yield, assumed about 9%, plus 1 point, up to management's 12% cost of capital). Other cases: $64-77 if growth matches the record 15%; $41-49 at 10% growth. About $5-6 per share of equity-method stakes in bottlers and the entertainment affiliate is not counted. The literal §5 net-working-capital test gives about $0 per share, so the stock fails it.
margin_of_safety: About 14-27% below base-case value at $46.56; 27-40% if record growth continues; roughly zero at 10% growth. No margin on the 1965 net-working-capital rule. The safety comes from how durable the franchise is (owner-earnings yield of 5.6% needs only about 3.5% perpetual growth to match a 9% bond), not from balance-sheet assets.

key_reasons.reason: The core business earns very high returns on equity with modest leverage. The improvement shows in return on equity, not just EPS growth.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Return on equity, not EPS growth, is the primary test (brk-letter-1979)
key_reasons.evidence: ROE about 20% with debt/capital of 3.5-15% in 1977-83; 27.2% in 1987 and about 33% in 1988; net debt only 15.3% of capital at YE1987; soft-drink segment pretax operating income/identifiable assets 34.3% in 1987, international 52.1% (ar-1987 Note 16; upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: A durable moat: a dominant trademark, scale and low-cost bottling, and pricing power that keeps the gains of cost and tax changes instead of passing them on.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §3 Durable competitive advantage: the moat around the castle (brk-letter-1986#16); franchise strength vs. price-competitive industries (brk-letter-1986#22)
key_reasons.evidence: Over 44% of world soft-drink sales, 1987 volume double the nearest competitor's; US share over 40% in 1988; US fountain share 59%, outselling the rival 2-to-1; flexible-pricing bottler contracts used in October 1986; Latin America operating income up 17% in 1988 on 1% volume growth; management states it can 'adjust prices to compensate for increasing costs' (ar-1986, ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: Owner earnings are close to reported earnings because the core needs little capital, so most of what is earned is available to owners.
key_reasons.evidence: 1987: net income $916M + depreciation $152M − capex $300M; core soft-drink capex $170M against over $1.4B of segment operating income; operating cash flow $1,231M; owner earnings estimated at $2.15-2.30 per share against $2.43 reported EPS (ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: Retained earnings have created far more than $1 of market value per $1 kept, and buybacks have been large and mostly well below value.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Each $1 retained must create at least $1 of market value (brk-letter-1983); buybacks only well below intrinsic value (brk-letter-1984#4)
key_reasons.evidence: About $5.93 per share retained from 1982-88 against a price rise from $11.58 to $46.56 (about $5.90 per $1; about $2.30 per $1 at a constant 8.9x multiple); about 69M shares repurchased in 1984-88 at 11.6-17.5x earnings; 40M-share program with about 14.5M shares remaining (ar-1986, ar-1987, upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: Management is in place, has corrected course (dropped the side businesses and narrowed to the core), and reports one-off items and currency effects openly.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §4 Honest, able management already in place; candid reporting (brk-letter-1979, brk-letter-1983#2)
key_reasons.evidence: Team assembled in 1981; 1986 gain ($375M) and provisions ($180M) shown separately; currency tailwinds quantified (27%, 16%, 10%); entertainment moved into a 49% affiliate; plastics, pasta and Embassy units sold; 1987 report: 'preferring investments within our existing lines of business' (ar-1986, ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: The price is sensible for an outstanding business. The expected return exceeds bonds and management's 12% cost of capital unless growth falls well below the record.
key_reasons.framework_principle: Outstanding business at a sensible price rather than a mediocre bargain (brk-letter-1987#18); price must make sense if the future resembles the past (brk-letter-1981#3)
key_reasons.evidence: $46.56 is 16.3x 1988 EPS of $2.85 and about 18x estimated owner earnings; 10-year owner's return about 13.5% at 13% growth with a 15x exit; EPS grew about 16% a year from 1983 to 1988; management guides to mid-teens EPS growth for 1989 (prices; upi-1989-01-31).

key_reasons.reason: A large but not maximum position is justified: the facts and the franchise's durability are very likely right, but the margin of safety is only moderate.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §7 Concentrate when the facts are clear (bpl-letter-1965); §2/§1 hunt elephants (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: About $17.3B market value allows a position of any size; 12-year uninterrupted earnings record; 26 consecutive dividend increases; base-case margin of safety only about 14-27% with the stock near its 52-week high of $49.12 (prices; ar-1987).

key_reasons.reason: No catalyst is needed. Value comes from compounding owner earnings, which the market eventually reflects.
key_reasons.framework_principle: §6 No catalyst needed: the market eventually reflects business results (brk-letter-1987)
key_reasons.evidence: Corporate restructurings (bottler IPOs, entertainment spin-off) are complete; this is not a work-out or a control situation; buybacks keep raising per-share value (ar-1987; upi-1989-01-31).

risks: Currency: about 74% of operating income comes from abroad, and the weak dollar of 1986-88 flattered growth. A stronger dollar would temporarily lower reported owner earnings.
Valuation depends on growth: at 10% per-share growth the stock is only about fairly priced, and at 7% it is overvalued. The margin of safety is moderate.
Capital allocation could slip back toward diversification (as with entertainment and foods) or toward leverage for financial structuring; management raised its net debt ceiling to 35%.
The bottling system earns low returns (bottling affiliate about 2-6% on net assets) and needs repeated equity support from the company.
Exposure to the entertainment affiliate: 1988 write-downs, $325M of receivables guaranteed with recourse, and $394M of other guarantees at YE1987.
The Puerto Rico tax exemption (worth about 4 points of tax rate) expires in 1995.
Gaps in the packet: no 1988 annual report, no proxy (insider ownership, pay), no maintenance capex split, no competitor cost data, no bond yield (assumed about 9%).
what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence that growth comes mostly from currency gains and buybacks rather than units and pricing, i.e. currency-neutral per-share owner-earnings growth below about 8-10%.
Market share losses to the primary competitor in the US fountain or international markets, or concentrate price discounting.
Management announcing a large acquisition outside soft drinks, or issuing stock to pay for one.
Buybacks continuing at prices well above intrinsic value (e.g. above about 25x owner earnings), or net debt rising toward the 35% ceiling to fund financial engineering.
In the 1988 annual report: capex well above depreciation in the core business, or larger contingent losses from the entertainment affiliate than disclosed.
Meeting management and finding a growth-for-its-own-sake or empire-building attitude, or low insider ownership and pay tied to size rather than returns.
A price drop toward $40 or below with the franchise intact would increase conviction and justify adding toward the 40% ceiling.
sell_triggers: The core franchise's economics turn out to have been misread: a sustained decline in soft-drink segment return on assets or loss of global share leadership (brk-letter-1987#18: easier to exit marketable securities when economics are misread).

Management shows itself indifferent to owners: stock-funded acquisitions that dilute value (brk-letter-1982#17), or abandoning share repurchases when they clearly favor owners while retaining earnings in sub-par uses (brk-letter-1984#4).
Retained earnings stop producing at least $1 of market value per $1 retained over a multi-year period (brk-letter-1983).
A high price alone is not a trigger. The default for this kind of business with these managers is to hold permanently (brk-letter-1987#18).
